Review Finds Digital Media and Artificial Intelligence Cannot Replace Maternal Dental Consultations

A comprehensive narrative review in Frontiers in Oral Health indicates that emerging generative artificial intelligence tools and digital platforms cannot replace professional dental guidance during pregnancy, despite their expanding accessibility. Synthesizing evidence from 1997 through September 2026, lead author Liliana Sachelarie and colleagues evaluated how digital media and large language models influence maternal oral health education. The researchers determined that while digital resources offer interactive educational opportunities, publicly accessible online materials exhibit substantial variability in scientific reliability, completeness, and clinical accuracy across platforms. Pregnancy induces critical physiological, hormonal, and behavioral shifts that heighten oral disease vulnerability, making reliable patient guidance vital. Nevertheless, popular digital channels frequently promote unsupported dental advice and omit clinical caveats. The review highlights that high public visibility, conversational fluency, and audience engagement metrics do not guarantee scientific veracity, warning that unsupervised artificial intelligence advice remains clinically unvalidated for pregnant patients seeking maternal healthcare.

Biological changes during gestation alter maternal susceptibility to oral pathology across multiple physiological pathways. Elevated circulating concentrations of estrogen and progesterone enhance gingival vascular permeability and amplify the inflammatory response of oral tissues to dental plaque, frequently contributing to pregnancy-associated gingivitis and exacerbating existing periodontal disease. Concurrently, altered dietary patterns, increased snacking frequency, cravings for fermentable carbohydrates, and modified salivary characteristics combine to heighten susceptibility to cariogenic activity. Recurrent nausea, vomiting, and gastroesophageal reflux repeatedly expose enamel to acidic gastric secretions, accelerating erosive tooth wear. The synthesis emphasizes that pregnancy does not inherently cause dental caries or spontaneous tooth loss. Rather, pathology develops through altered oral hygiene habits, dietary shifts, and deferred preventive care. Maintaining rigorous daily plaque control through regular brushing with fluoride toothpaste, interdental cleaning, dietary discipline, and timely professional dental monitoring remains an essential preventive foundation throughout gestation.

Despite clear biological needs, dental care remains heavily underused among pregnant individuals due to pervasive misconceptions regarding fetal harm. Systematic appraisals of maternal beliefs reveal widespread fallacies, including convictions that dental interventions harm the unborn child, that clinical visits must be deferred until after birth, and that the developing fetus leaches calcium directly from maternal dentition. In contrast, authoritative consensus guidance from the American Dental Association and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists confirms that routine evaluations, cleanings, diagnostic radiography, and indicated restorative procedures can be safely administered across all gestational stages. Standard oral local anesthetics, including lidocaine formulated with epinephrine, are safe when administered at clinical dosages. The review authors note that unwarranted treatment avoidance represents a severe health threat, permitting localized periodontal inflammation or untreated caries to escalate into acute infections, persistent maternal pain, and complex dental emergencies that compromise general maternal wellbeing.

To prevent severe enamel loss from recurrent nausea and vomiting, clinical evidence outlines specific post-emetic hygiene behaviors that challenge intuitive patient habits. Mechanical toothbrushing immediately following an emetic episode causes significant surface damage, as abrasive bristles abrade enamel softened by contact with gastric acid. Nutritional education must likewise emphasize the frequency of acid exposure and carbohydrate intake rather than total volume alone. Unfortunately, maternal awareness regarding these protective strategies remains deficient across evaluated populations. Educational gaps encompass periodontal pathology, caries prevention, and the safety of dental local anesthesia. Traditional clinical encounters frequently fail to bridge these knowledge deficits due to restricted consultation times, variable baseline health literacy, and limited patient retention, driving many pregnant women toward online platforms for reassurance.

The migration of pregnant individuals toward digital channels has transformed health communication, yet visual platforms frequently fail to deliver reliable guidance. Video repositories like YouTube feature extensive content regarding pregnancy oral health, but formal analyses show severe qualitative deficiencies. Investigations by Çardakcı Bahar and colleagues, along with research by Yegül and associates, established that pregnancy-related dental videos exhibit profound variability in scientific accuracy, completeness, and educational merit. Consequently, highly viewed and heavily shared media often promote inaccurate dental advice. The researchers stress that high visibility and engagement metrics do not signify educational validity, presenting serious challenges for pregnant users seeking credible maternal healthcare information.

Structured mobile health interventions provide more targeted educational support, though their clinical superiority remains unproven. Empirical studies examining mobile text-messaging programs during pregnancy demonstrate measurable gains in maternal oral health knowledge, self-care attitudes, personal self-efficacy, and dental plaque scores. However, comparative investigations indicate that altering message-framing strategies produces no meaningful difference in patient outcomes, and text messaging has not demonstrated global superiority over conventional clinical education. Similarly, prototype mobile applications tailored to maternal oral health demonstrate favorable usability and acceptability scores among pregnant participants and expert dental reviewers. Nonetheless, the review highlights that high usability ratings do not equate to demonstrated clinical effectiveness. These observations underscore that while mHealth provides valuable communication channels, technological delivery alone does not ensure clinical efficacy.

Evaluating the scientific integrity of digital health content requires distinct methodological tools, as structural quality and factual accuracy represent separate constructs. Standardized instruments such as the DISCERN tool appraise consumer health information regarding treatment alternatives, while the four JAMA benchmarks evaluate publication transparency through authorship, attribution, disclosure, and currency. Readability formulas, including Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level metrics, assess linguistic complexity, demonstrating marked reading difficulty across online dental literature. In addition, the Global Quality Score evaluates overall educational utility and presentation flow. However, a cited scoping review emphasizes that these instruments measure presentational attributes rather than detecting false clinical claims without substituting for thorough clinical review. Misinformation must be identified through direct comparison against established clinical evidence and professional consensus guidelines. Differentiating between readability, presentation quality, and factual accuracy is essential to determine whether digital health educational materials safely support maternal decision-making.
